analysis.one_liner: Strengthens federal anti-discrimination law, lets victims sue over discriminatory policies in court instead of forced arbitration, and ends qualified immunity.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with one cosponsor in the House on October 21, 2022, never received a hearing or a vote and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The Justice for All Act of 2022 would have rewritten major federal civil rights laws. It would have let people sue over policies that have a discriminatory effect (disparate impact) on the basis of race, sex, national origin, age, or disability — restoring a right the Supreme Court took away in 2001 in Alexander v. Sandoval. It would have banned companies from forcing workers, consumers, and civil rights plaintiffs into private arbitration or blocking class actions, made employers directly liable for their employees' harassment and discrimination, ended qualified immunity for officials who violate the Constitution, banned police profiling, and expanded anti-discrimination rules to cover sexual orientation, gender identity, pregnancy, and natural Black hairstyles in housing, schools, stores, and transit. The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, workers facing workplace harassment, tenants facing housing discrimination, consumers and employees forced into arbitration clauses, Black workers affected by hair discrimination, LGBTQ people facing discrimination in public accommodations and federally funded programs, and victims of police profiling would have gained enforceable court rights, including damages and attorney's fees, against employers, governments, and businesses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, tenants, consumers, civil rights plaintiffs

how_it_helps.text: Restores the right of individuals to sue in federal court over policies that have a discriminatory effect on the basis of race, sex, national origin, age, or disability — a right the Supreme Court removed in Alexander v. Sandoval (2001) — with compensatory and punitive damages and attorney's fees available.

Bans companies from forcing workers, consumers, and civil rights plaintiffs into private arbitration and from barring them from joining class actions, so claims can be heard in open court or as group lawsuits.
Removes the Faragher-Ellerth defense so employers can no longer escape sexual harassment liability simply by showing they had a policy and that the victim failed to use it.

Ends qualified immunity in 42 U.S.C. 1983 suits, allowing citizens to recover from federal, state, and local officials who violate their constitutional rights, and extends 1983 to actions taken under color of federal law.

Explicitly defines sex discrimination to include pregnancy, sexual orientation, gender identity, and sex characteristics, defines race discrimination to include natural hair texture and protective hairstyles, extends public accommodations protections to stores, transit, airlines, and online retailers, and prohibits law enforcement profiling.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, landlords, schools and universities, retailers and service providers, and state and local governments — including police agencies — would bear new liability exposure, litigation costs, and compliance requirements, and would lose forced arbitration as a shield against civil rights claims.

drawbacks.text: Employers would be strictly liable for any discrimination or harassment committed by any employee, and the existing defense that an employer took reasonable preventive and corrective action would be eliminated — a cost businesses and some advocates would call unfair, even when the employer acted responsibly.

The bill would end qualified immunity, making federal, state, and local officials — including police — personally subject to damages suits for constitutional violations, which government and law enforcement groups argue would expose individual officers and public budgets to extensive litigation.

The new disparate-impact standard and expanded public accommodations rules would apply to schools, transit systems, retailers, and landlords, increasing compliance and litigation costs that could be passed on or, in the case of governments, borne by taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would have been real for people whose civil rights claims are currently dismissed or forced into secret arbitration, including victims of harassment whose employers can currently escape liability by showing they had anti-harassment policies. The costs an honest supporter would acknowledge are real too: making employers strictly liable for every employee's conduct, ending qualified immunity, and allowing disparate-impact suits against any public program would generate substantial litigation against schools, housing providers, and local governments, and courts or the next Congress might not sustain such a broad rewrite. Whether that cost is worth the restored access to court is a genuine policy judgment, and the bill got no debate on it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on October 21, 2022 and referred to the House Judiciary and Education and Labor Committees, neither of which acted on it before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on October 21, 2022, less than three months before the Congress ended, and referred to the Judiciary and Education and Labor Committees.
No committee action, hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the action history; the bill sat in committee until the 117th Congress expired on January 3, 2023, at which point it died.
Only one Democratic cosponsor joined the sponsor, and no Republican supported it, so there was no cross-party base of support to pressure committee chairs to act.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses, government bodies, and law enforcement agencies that would have faced expanded civil rights liability — and whose interests the committees that never acted on the bill were positioned to reflect — are better off because it died.

for.name: Cori Bush
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the only cosponsor.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 21, 2022 and took no action — no hearing, markup, or report — before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Received a concurrent referral on October 21, 2022 and took no action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got to a vote, but its support was entirely Democratic — the sponsor and its single cosponsor were both progressive House Democrats — with no Republican cosponsor recorded.

industries.note: The bill would strip forced arbitration and class-action waivers, impose strict liability for employee harassment and discrimination, and remove the Faragher-Ellerth defense, making workplace civil rights suits far easier to bring and win.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies and police unions
industries.note: A federal profiling ban with private enforcement and the end of qualified immunity would expose individual officers and departments to civil suits for stops and searches.

Federally funded programs and state and local governments could face disparate-impact discrimination suits and, for political subdivisions, liability for officials' constitutional violations; only punitive damages against governments would remain unavailable.

industries.industry: Forced-arbitration-dependent industries (finance, telecom, retail, gig employers)
industries.note: By making predispute arbitration and class-waiver clauses unenforceable for employment, consumer, and civil rights disputes, the bill would remove the private dispute-resolution system many consumer-facing industries rely on to keep claims out of court.
